So much of the pleasure of The Housemaid is about watching Seyfried peel back the layers of own character, unraveling and rebuilding herself before your eyes. First, she's a perfect, sweet, wealthy housewife. Then, she's a snippy, controlling, neurotic mistress of the house, doling out harsh punishments, unreasonable demands, and facilitating Millie's degradation. Then, her history is revealed as the long-suffering victim of her husband's torture and control. Finally, her scheme is revealed, and she's shown to be a supremely clever, resourceful woman who knows the game she's found herself in and knows how to play it. But all of that is just plot. Seyfried took this sleazy, pulpy movie and saw the humanity in the character at its center.

blocks.x: Seyfried clearly understands the ways people mask, perform, and protect themselves. Seyfried plays Nina's trauma and resulting fragility with a sharp eye for the ways psychological violence can break a person down. On top of that, she plays Nina's intentional deceptions and schemes fiercely, never flinching from being detestable or ferocious, embracing complexity. The troubling thing about Nina is that she sees the ways that Millie is vulnerable to abuse and takes advantage of them, much like her husband did to her. She does this to get herself and her daughter out of a terrible situation, but she knows she's putting Millie at risk to do so. Nina is no villain, but it's hard to call her a hero. Seyfried plays into this duality in a remarkably truthful performance. She's fully embodied in everything from her walk and posture to micro-expressions.

Amanda Seyfried is a powerhouse, carrying the success of The Housemaid. Without her, The Housemaid's Secret risks losing the complexity that made it so successful. While Sweeney has a perfectly good performance in The Housemaid, especially given the subdued, casual persona of her character, she has put out much more commanding performances before. One example was in the similarly-themed Christy, the biopic of boxer Christy Martin and her abusive relationship with her coach. Though Christy was a box office failure, Sweeney's performance received critical acclaim. Sweeney can certainly act, and The Housemaid's Secret promises to reveal Millie's layers. One can hope it will yield a richer, more embodied performance for Sweeney, and a movie that doesn't need Amanda Seyfried's magnetism to succeed.
